units: a newly learned idea leaves a trace that is at first unstable
that trace settles mainly during sleep
the nerve circuits replay the learned sequence during that phase
reviewing too soon after learning brings almost no benefit
a little forgetting before the review strengthens its effect
recalling without help fixes the material better than rereading it
specialists advise stretching the gap between two passes
writing the idea down and then trying to say it back from memory produces lasting knowledge
text: Understanding an idea in class is not the end of learning it. At first the brain turns what it takes in into a faint trace, and that trace wipes out easily. The slower work comes later, mostly while you sleep: nerve circuits replay the sequence you picked up and settle it into place. Go back over the material right away and you gain almost nothing, because the trace is still fresh. Wait until a little of it has slipped away, and the review forces your memory to rebuild what it lost. Pulling the answer back with no help does far more than reading the page again. That is why people who study learning tell you to stretch the gap between one pass and the next. Write the idea down, put the card away, then try to say it back with nothing in front of you. What you keep that way stays.

units: a bookbinding shop nearly stopped operating
its last craftsman lost the use of one of his hands
the moves of the trade had never been written down
the woman in charge had him recorded while he described each operation
an apprentice carried out the moves while he corrected her out loud
the outcome was a manual naming the most common fault at every step
the shop kept working and drew applicants from far away
one man's accident set off the writing down of a practice that had been spoken until then
text: A bookbinding shop came close to shutting down when its last craftsman lost the use of one hand. Nobody had ever written the small maneuvers of the trade down, and the woman running the place was afraid the whole repertoire would vanish along with him. So she set a recorder running and had him talk through every operation: sewing the folded sheets, gluing the spine, setting the headbands, paring the leather. An apprentice did the work with her hands while his voice caught her mistakes as they surfaced. Out of that arrangement came a manual nobody had planned, with a note beside each step naming the error people make there most often. The shop stayed open, and the manual brought in applicants from distant regions. One man's injury had pushed a craft that lived only in speech onto the page.

units: the words are missing at the moment of saying back what has been noted
the method proposed rests on a notebook kept for this alone
each page is divided into two columns of unequal width
the wide column takes the word met and a whole sentence that carries it
the narrow column takes a definition written by the learner himself
a mark is added every week the word still slips away
the words piling up too many marks are copied apart and gone over out loud
at the end of a season the notebook forms a word list belonging to its author
text: Your notes accumulate and nothing fastens itself to them. The moment you have to say any of it back, the words desert you. The remedy is modest: a single notebook, reserved for nothing else. Rule every page into two columns of unequal width, a broad one and a slender one. In the broad column, set down the word you ran into and a whole sentence that carries it. In the narrow one, write a short definition in your own wording, never lifted from somewhere else. Any week the word still slips away from you, add a mark beside it. Once a page carries too many marks, copy those stubborn words onto a fresh sheet and work through them standing up and out loud, with the definition kept out of sight. By the end of a season the notebook has turned into a glossary that belongs to nobody but you.

units: two neighborhood workshops announce the same goal of repairing on your own
the first workshop runs in the shape of a lecture
the people at the first leave with papers they will never open again
the second workshop is built around the machines brought in by those who come
there you move ahead by sitting next to someone who has already taken a similar machine apart
the organizers of the second admit that their approach is confused and noisy
the people at the second come back while those at the first grow scarce
the gap between the two workshops comes from where the question starts
text: Two neighborhood workshops make the same offer: learn to repair on your own whatever breaks down at home. The first runs like a lecture. An instructor stands at the front, holds up the tools, hands out a printed guide, and everyone leaves with a stack of paper they will never open again. The second runs like a work site. You show up with your own broken machine, sit down beside a person who has already taken one like it apart, and follow the thread of your own breakdown until it loosens. The people behind the second workshop are the first to admit their setup is loud, disorderly, and hard to measure. Their crowd comes back the following week, though, while attendance at the lecture thins out by the third session. The gap has nothing to do with the equipment. It lies in who asks the question.

units: a smell of white dust catches you as soon as you enter the room
a worn raised platform carries a narrow table and a chair that does not match
a dark board covers the full width of the wall and keeps lines that cannot be wiped off
the school desks lined up keep a hollow groove now out of use
notches were cut into the wood by impatient hands
boxes of yellowed writings are piled on the ledge of the openings
a glass cabinet holds rolled maps a skeleton and jars
the room now serves as storage without anything having been taken out of it
text: Push the door open and the smell of chalk dust reaches you before anything else. At the back, a low platform worn smooth by shoe leather carries a narrow table and a chair that never matched it. A black slate runs the whole width of the wall, streaked with pale lines no cloth will take off anymore. The desks stand in rows of six, each one keeping its hollow groove for ink, dry for years now, and its notches cut by restless hands with a knife. Boxes of yellowed exercises are stacked along the window ledges, every page covered in careful writing. Behind glass, a cabinet holds rolled maps, a wooden skeleton, and dusty jars whose labels are peeling off. Nothing was thrown out and nothing was replaced. The room is a storeroom now, and people step into it the way you step into a memory left open.

units: the ease of deleting a word harms the teaching of writing
the pupil of earlier days left the mark of his hesitations on his page
the first draft counted as proof of a path of thought
the coming of electronic supports made correction invisible
a deleted mistake can no longer be read again by its author
you get better by going back over what you missed and not by handing in a clean copy
the teacher deprived of the first draft judges nothing but an endpoint
the writer argues for giving correction marks their standing back
text: Deleting a word costs nothing now, and the teaching of writing has lost more by that than anyone reckons. A pupil used to write in ink, so the page held on to every hesitation: a crossed-out line, a word called back in the margin, a sentence begun again two lines further down. The draft was not waste. It was evidence that thinking had happened. Then came the electronic screens, where a correction leaves no scar at all. The mistake goes, and the chance of ever reading it again goes with it. Nobody gets better by handing in an immaculate copy. You get better by going back to what you missed. A teacher who sees only the finished version has no view of the mind at work; he grades an arrival and forfeits the journey. Give the crossing-out its standing back and you give error its use as a tool.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman teaching the workshop worked earlier as a potter
a joint condition forced her to give up the wheel
that injury is the reason she moved into teaching
she can no longer show a movement over a long stretch
she therefore cut every movement into short steps named with precision
her students get a vocabulary that other workshops leave unspoken
her apprentices move ahead faster than those trained by imitation alone
being able to describe a fault before correcting it explains that lead
text: The woman who teaches the pottery workshop spent the greater part of her working life at the wheel herself. Inflamed wrist joints put an end to that, and it was the injury that pushed her toward teaching. Since she can no longer sustain a demonstration over any length of time, she had to break every movement into short steps and give each of them an exact name: centering, opening, raising the wall, smoothing. Her students walk away with a vocabulary that most workshops leave unspoken. This insistence on words has had an effect she never planned on. Her apprentices come along faster than apprentices trained by imitation alone, because they can put a name to what went wrong before they fix it. The physical trouble of a single woman changed the way an entire trade gets taught.

units: the book of exercises is aimed at apprentice carpenters
its physical making and its drawings are judged to be of good quality
the rising order of difficulty looks carefully thought through
the book shows nothing but successful moves and never failed ones
a learner who gets it wrong finds no page describing his fault
that absence leads the learner to lay the failure on himself alone
the reviewer suggests adding a picture of the botched piece on the facing page
he also suggests joining to that picture the question to ask in front of it
text: The book of exercises written for apprentice carpenters has a flaw that its handsome manufacture does not buy off. The binding holds, the drawings are clean, the climb in difficulty has clearly been thought through at length. Where it fails is decisive: it displays the cut that works and never the cut that goes astray. An apprentice whose line wanders off finds no page telling him what a mistake looks like, or what it does to the joint once the pieces meet. Too often he concludes that the failure belongs to him alone. Putting this right would be straightforward and inexpensive. Facing every plate, add a picture of the botched piece, and under it the question to ask yourself when you are looking at one. That much would turn a handsome object into an instrument you could genuinely learn from.

units: the reader is torn between evening lessons and going straight into an apprenticeship
the writer of the letter took both roads
the evening teaching announces its program and marks the exercises
on that road a failure costs nothing but a harsh comment
the workshop announces nothing and there you learn by starting over after failing
a mistake made in the workshop is paid for in wasted material
the writer advises beginning with the evening lessons
he recommends noting down what you fail to understand in a notebook before turning up at the workshop
craftsmen gladly take in a newcomer who carries precise questions
text: You asked me whether to sign up for the evening class or go straight into a workshop. I took both roads, and the difference has stayed with me. In the class you move lesson by lesson: the program is laid out in advance, the exercises come back marked, and failing costs you nothing worse than a hard comment. You pick up the principles quickly, but the material stays at arm's length. In the workshop nothing is announced. You watch, you ruin things, you start over, and every mistake is paid for in wasted stock. What you gain there is a confidence no lesson hands you. My advice is short. Begin with the class, keep a notebook of everything that stays unclear, then turn up at the workshop with those pages. Craftsmen open right up to anyone who arrives with a real question. Write and tell me what you decide.

units: the question asked bears on what separates a trainer who marks you from a trainer you forget
the woman running a retraining center puts the difference down to patience with repetition
she names first the listening that lets the learner finish his wrong statement
she names next the cutting of the task into pieces small enough to keep failure away
she names the negative example where the trainer himself performs the faulty move in front of everyone
she names last the silence held while the learner is searching for the answer
the poor trainer talks too much and moves ahead too fast
he takes the clarity of his own explanation for the understanding of his audience
she states that you turn into a trainer by watching other people get it wrong
text: What makes one trainer stay with you for years while another leaves nothing behind? The woman who runs a retraining center answers without a pause: patience with hearing the same thing twice. Then she breaks it down. Listening comes first, since a good trainer lets the learner finish the wrong sentence instead of cutting in. Next comes the slicing: the task is cut into pieces so small that failure hardly gets a chance. Then the bad example, performed by the trainer in front of everyone and owned. Last comes the silence, held while the learner is closing in on it. And the poor trainer? He talks too much, pushes ahead too fast, and takes the clarity of his own explanation for understanding in the room. She adds one thing. Nobody turns into a trainer by reciting. You turn into one by watching other people go wrong.
